# **Smart Reading: FPGA-Based Assistive Glasses and Rapid Processing Research for Dyslexia**

### **A Project Proposal for the Learn Through Discovery Projects Hatchery**

California State Polytechnic University, Pomona

**Faculty Mentor:** Dr. Mohamed El Hadedy, Department of Electrical & Computer Engineering

---

## **Project Summary**

The Smart Reading Project reimagines how individuals with dyslexia interact with written information by combining **biomedical research and engineering innovation**. This initiative proposes a two-pronged approach:

1. Conducting undergraduate-led research on the effects of **rapid reading techniques on individuals with dyslexia**, and  
2. Developing **FPGA-powered augmented reality (AR) smart glasses** that implement **Rapid Serial Visual Presentation (RSVP)** to improve reading speed and comprehension.

Dyslexia affects approximately 5–20% of the population and is characterized by difficulties in decoding, word recognition, and reading fluency. These challenges are not simply educational barriers—they impact access to information, academic success, and professional opportunities. Recent research shows that individuals with dyslexia exhibit **longer fixation durations, shorter saccades, and more frequent regressions**, indicating a more effortful and inefficient visual sampling strategy when reading (Franzen et al., 2024). These findings suggest that reading difficulty is not only linguistic but also tied to **how visual information is processed over time**.

At the same time, emerging evidence demonstrates that **reading performance can improve when individuals are guided to read faster under controlled conditions**. Training methods that impose time constraints have been shown to significantly improve reading speed and comprehension—even in adults with persistent dyslexia—by enhancing rapid information processing (Breznitz et al., 2013). This suggests that reading deficits are not fixed, but can be mitigated through optimized presentation of information.

Our project bridges these insights by designing a system that **changes how text is delivered to the reader** rather than forcing the reader to adapt to traditional text formats. Using FPGA-based hardware, we will develop smart glasses that present text using RSVP—displaying words sequentially at a controlled rate to reduce eye movement demands, eliminate inefficient scanning patterns, and improve processing efficiency.

This project is both a **research platform and an assistive technology prototype**. It empowers students across engineering, biology, and pre-med disciplines to collaborate on a real-world problem at the intersection of **neuroscience, human-computer interaction, and embedded systems**. Ultimately, our goal is to create a scalable, open-source framework for assistive reading technologies that can improve accessibility and reshape how we think about reading in the modern world.

---

## **Project Background and Solution**

Reading is a complex process requiring precise coordination between **visual perception, eye movements, and cognitive processing**. During normal reading, the eyes alternate between fixations (brief pauses to process text) and saccades (rapid jumps between words). Efficient readers process text quickly, with fixations lasting approximately 225–250 ms and saccades spanning 7–9 characters (Franzen et al., 2024).

However, individuals with dyslexia exhibit fundamentally different reading behavior. Studies show they:

* Spend **more time per fixation**  
* Make **shorter eye movements (saccades)**  
* Fixate on more words and skip fewer words  
* Exhibit **irregular eye movement patterns**, including atypical directional deviations

These patterns indicate a **laborious and inefficient visual sampling strategy**, where more time and effort are required to extract the same information (Franzen et al., 2024). Importantly, these inefficiencies are not solely due to comprehension deficits but are linked to **slower lexical processing and reduced reading fluency**.

Traditional interventions often focus on phonological training, but they do not fully address the **temporal and visual dynamics of reading**. Furthermore, research on reading performance highlights that **sequential reading itself introduces cognitive load**, especially for individuals with dyslexia. The need to process words in order, coordinate eye movements, and maintain context creates what researchers describe as a “compounding burden” on performance (Conforti et al., 2024).

Recent findings offer a promising alternative: modifying how text is presented. Rapid Serial Visual Presentation (RSVP) removes the need for eye movements by presenting words one at a time at a fixed location. This directly addresses inefficiencies in visual sampling by:

* Eliminating saccades and regressions  
* Reducing fixation variability  
* Allowing controlled pacing of information flow

Additionally, studies show that **forcing faster reading speeds under structured conditions improves both reading speed and comprehension**, even in dyslexic adults (Breznitz et al., 2013). This suggests that **processing speed is a key bottleneck** and can be trained or augmented.

Our solution integrates these insights into a unified system:

* A **research study** to quantify how RSVP and speed constraints affect dyslexic readers  
* A **hardware platform (FPGA smart glasses)** that delivers text in an optimized format

Unlike existing assistive tools (e.g., overlays, fonts), which show inconsistent effectiveness, our approach targets the **core mechanism of reading inefficiency: temporal processing and eye movement behavior**.

---

## **Objectives, Timeline, and Goals**

### **Primary Objective**

To design, prototype, and validate an FPGA-powered smart glasses system that improves reading performance in individuals with dyslexia through optimized text presentation.

---

### **Project Phases**

#### **Phase 1: Research Design and Literature Integration**

* Develop experimental protocols for testing RSVP and speed-reading interventions  
* Define measurable metrics (reading speed, comprehension, fixation behavior)  
* Align engineering requirements with research goals

**Deliverables:** Study design, IRB preparation (if applicable), system requirements

---

#### **Phase 2: System Architecture and Simulation**

* Design FPGA-based text rendering pipeline  
* Develop RSVP algorithms with adjustable speeds  
* Simulate display timing and latency

**Deliverables:** HDL models, RSVP timing framework

---

#### **Phase 3: Prototype Development (Milestone 1\)**

* Build FPGA-based wearable display system  
* Integrate microdisplay or HUD optics  
* Implement real-time text streaming

**Deliverables:** Functional smart glasses prototype

---

#### **Phase 4: Experimental Testing and Data Collection**

* Conduct user studies with participants (control \+ dyslexia groups)  
* Compare traditional reading vs RSVP performance  
* Measure reading speed (WPM), comprehension, and fatigue

**Deliverables:** Dataset, preliminary analysis

---

#### **Phase 5: Optimization and System Integration (Milestone 2\)**

* Refine display timing and UI  
* Optimize comfort and usability  
* Integrate adaptive reading speeds

**Deliverables:** Improved prototype with adaptive features

---

#### **Phase 6: Final Validation and Dissemination (Milestone 3\)**

* Final testing and validation  
* Publish findings and open-source designs  
* Create onboarding materials for future students

**Deliverables:** Final report, research paper, GitHub repository

---

## **SMART Goals**

### **Specific**

Develop a wearable smartglasses system for dyslexic individuals through improving reading efficiency by reducing reliance on inefficient eye movement patterns and enhancing processing speed.

### **Measurable**

* Increase reading speed (WPM) compared to baseline  
* Maintain or improve comprehension scores  
* Reduce fixation-related inefficiencies (via indirect metrics like time per word)

### **Attainable**

Supported by interdisciplinary collaboration across engineering and biomedical fields, existing FPGA tools, and established research frameworks.

### **Relevant**

Addresses both a **major educational accessibility issue** and a **gap in assistive technology design**. Also produces interdisciplinary work where students can gain knowledge and experience in relevant topics.

### **Time-Bound**

* Research \+ Design: Months 1–2  
* Prototype Development: Months 3–5  
* Testing \+ Optimization: Months 6–7  
* Finalization: Month 8

---

## **Broader Impact**

This project extends beyond a single device. It introduces a **new paradigm for reading accessibility**, shifting the focus from modifying the reader to modifying the **information delivery system**.

Educational Impact:

* Provides hands-on research opportunities for engineering and pre-med students  
* Bridges neuroscience and embedded systems

Technological Impact:

* Demonstrates FPGA use in human-centered computing  
* Enables modular, open-source assistive tech

Societal Impact:

* Improves accessibility for millions of individuals with dyslexia  
* Reduces barriers to education and information access

---

## **Conclusion**

The Smart Reading Project represents a convergence of **science, engineering, and accessibility**. By leveraging research on eye movements, cognitive processing, and rapid reading techniques, we aim to build a system that fundamentally improves how people with dyslexia engage with text.

This is more than a device—it is a **platform for rethinking reading itself**.

The Case For Quick Processing Techniques ([https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms2488](https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms2488))

* Poor reading skills of developmental dyslexics persist into adulthood with standard remediation protocols having little effect. Nevertheless, reading improves if readers are induced to read faster. Here we show that this improvement can be enhanced by training. Training follows a multi-session procedure adapted to silent sentence reading, with individually set, increasingly more demanding, time constraints (letter-by-letter masking). In both typical and dyslexic adult readers, reading times are shortened and comprehension improves. After training, the dyslexic readers’ performance is similar to that of typical readers; moreover, their connected text reading times and comprehension scores significantly improve in standard reading tests and are retained at 6 months post training. Identical training without time constraints proves ineffective. Our results suggest that fluent reading depends in part on rapid information processing, which then might affect perception, cognitive processing and possibly eye movements. These processes remain malleable in adulthood, even in individuals with developmental dyslexia.

Specifically, data in California indicate:[4](https://edpolicyinca.org/publications/californias-adoption-reading-difficulties-risk-screening#footnote4_xFSccYSpasXSDyAiD41ZgYvZiPaEwvu0H3QiFKf9V2k_zvgNu2YFbfrs) only 49 percent of all students met or exceeded proficiency in English language arts on the [2024–25 California Assessment of Student Performance and Progress](https://www.cde.ca.gov/nr/ne/yr25/yr25rel43.asp) (CAASPP); only 44 percent of all third graders and 15 percent of third graders identified as English learner (ELs) met or exceeded standards on the 2024–25 CAASPP; and despite marginal growth after the COVID-19 pandemic, California students’ scores remain below prepandemic levels.[5](https://edpolicyinca.org/publications/californias-adoption-reading-difficulties-risk-screening#footnote5_2hkCptGK6vtNXIn9voeum-LY0EArASHtKF4DeInN0_ikRjICkA7swo) *Reading difficulty* is a broad term that may denote different conditions with different implications. Although universal screening targets only a risk for potential reading difficulties, advocates for children and families support screening as an important tool for identifying and tailoring proactive support for students who may be diagnosed with persistent word-reading disabilities like dyslexia. Diagnosed language-based learning disabilities are common and exist worldwide. Facts related to reading disabilities and dyslexia include the following: One in five children has a learning disability, and 34 percent of students receiving special education services in the United States are diagnosed with a specific learning disability related to reading, writing, and math.[6](https://edpolicyinca.org/publications/californias-adoption-reading-difficulties-risk-screening#footnote6_Cus0omZrPfPXNXC8mZ-eOVVHPkZHC2FPFVnpcalkfJ4_us8DpmqLTfLF) Dyslexia, “a severe and persistent difficulty learning to read (and spell) words despite adequate opportunity and instruction”[7](https://edpolicyinca.org/publications/californias-adoption-reading-difficulties-risk-screening#footnote7_cvSREoPGii0LHcOAqbbYrnntCKLYeQtLkaOjfEvnSQA_uaCdobPDdf0Q) affects approximately 5–17 percent of children.[8](https://edpolicyinca.org/publications/californias-adoption-reading-difficulties-risk-screening#footnote8_A20FYU6faeKLdr7DxZ6TDWBPFo9cwjG0vWn4V8QtoY_aYG5dSd3fOyg) About 85 percent of children with a learning disability have difficulty with reading and language.[9](https://edpolicyinca.org/publications/californias-adoption-reading-difficulties-risk-screening#footnote9_KWosXLMQu8WRy5d5vrJOyY2NjB6PVjzVF9P3JkFdY_z0uWvqCNqnIl)  |

| How prevalent dyslexia is depends upon the severity or cut-off used for identification. Common estimates of the prevalence of dyslexia fall in the range of 3 to 7 percent when specifying a criterion of scoring 1.5 standard deviations or more below the mean on measures of reading ([Fletcher et al., 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8183124/#R13), Peterson & Pennington, 2012; Snowling & Melby-Lervag, 2016). Similar estimates have been attained from cross-cultural studies ([Moll, Kuntz, Neuhoff, Bruder, & Shulte-Korne, 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8183124/#R27); [Snowling & Melby-Lervag, 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8183124/#R33)). Prevalence estimates are higher when the cut-off used for identification is less stringent. For example, by applying a cut-off of scoring at the 25th percentile in reading (which corresponds to approximately two-thirds of a standard deviation) and/or an IQ-achievement regression-based definition of 1.5 standard deviations, prevalence was estimated to be 17.4 percent of the school-age population ([Shaywitz et al., 1992](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8183124/#R32)). However, most estimates of prevalence fall below 10 percent ([Hoeft, McCardle, & Pugh, 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8183124/#R21)). For an example of using a Bayesian model to estimate the probability of the presence of dyslexia, Wagner et al. (2019) operationally defined dyslexia as scoring at or below the 5th percentile on a factor score from the Spencer et al. (2014) study based on the four indicators of poor decoding, impoverished sight word vocabulary, poor response to instruction, and listening comprehension better than reading comprehension. Because they chose to define dyslexia as scoring at or below the 5th percentile, the prior probability of having dyslexia was 5 percent. They updated the prior probability based on additional data. For example, if the individual is female, the chance of having dyslexia goes down, from 5 to 3 percent; if male, the chance goes up, from 5 to 7 percent. Co-occurring ADHD increases the chances of having dyslexia fourfold, from 5 to 19 percent. Scoring at or below the 20th percentile on a battery of first-grade predictors triples the chances of having dyslexia, from 5 to 15 percent. Having an affected parent or sibling increases the chances fivefold, from 5 to 26 percent. Combinations of risk factors result in considerably more risk. For example, being male with ADHD increases the chances from 5 to 24 percent. Add in an affected parent or sibling and the chances increase to 76 percent. Finally, add in scoring low on the predictor battery and chances increase to 92 percent (Wagner et al., 2019)\! Turning to potential correlates, ADHD co-occurs with reading disability from 30 to 50 percent of the time (Willcutt et al., 2003), and co-occurring math disability more than doubles the chances of having dyslexia (Joyner & Wagner, 2020). The prevalence of severe reading disability also is greater for males than females, with the ratio of males to females increasing with the severity of the reading problem (Quinn and Wagner, 2015). The earliest cases involved acquired dyslexia, which refers typically to adults who learned how to read but could no longer read after a stroke or traumatic brain injury despite being otherwise intact. Subsequently, children with apparent cases of developmental dyslexia were described who were unable to learn to read despite being able to do mathematics and who did not suffer from obvious brain injury. |

| Today, studies suggest that as many as 20% of people in the United States have dyslexia, which accounts for up to 90% of learning disabilities (Shaywitz, S. E., et al.,Current Opinion in Psychiatry, Vol. 34, No. 2, 2021opens in new window). Through studies of brains, genetics, and educational strategies, scientists are better understanding causes of reading troubles. But disagreement, debate, and misunderstandings rage on about many details, including how to define dyslexia, how to diagnose it, and how best to teach reading to struggling readers. These disagreements often incorporate politics as well as science. Still, dyslexia often goes unidentified. In a sample of close to 10,000 fourth graders in Italy, nearly 2 out of 3 students with the disorder had not been diagnosed ([Barbiero, C., et al., *PLOS ONE*, Vol. 14, No. 1, 2019opens in new window](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0210448)). Despite legislation in most U.S. states that governs screening, intervention, and other dyslexia-related services, non-White students and children who go to schools with predominantly non-White populations are also less likely than others to get diagnosed via dyslexia screening programs, Odegard and colleagues found in an analysis of data from 7,947 second-grade students in 126 schools in Arkansas ([*Journal of Learning Disabilities*, Vol. 53, No. 5, 2020opens in new window](https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219420914551)). Students attending majority-White schools, on the other hand, had access to more reading supports than other schools, found research in Boston, according to an article in the [*Hechinger Report*opens in new window](https://hechingerreport.org/while-white-students-get-specialists-struggling-black-and-latino-readers-often-left-on-their-own/), an education publication[.opens in new window](https://hechingerreport.org/while-white-students-get-specialists-struggling-black-and-latino-readers-often-left-on-their-own/) Those disparities reflect and likely exacerbate gaps in reading ability, studies suggest. According to [2022 data from the National Assessment of Educational Progressopens in new window](https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/reading/nation/achievement/?grade=4), just 33% of fourth-grade students and 31% of eighth-grade students are at or above proficiency levels in reading. Proficiency levels were 38% for White eighth graders compared with 16% for their Black classmates. Some of those children are likely to have dyslexia and other learning disorders and would benefit from extra intervention.  |

| How widespread is dyslexia? About 13–14% of the school population nationwide has a handicapping condition that qualifies them for special education. Current studies indicate that one half of all the students who qualify for special education are classified as having a learning disability (LD) (6–7%). About 85% of those students have a primary learning disability in reading and language processing. Nevertheless, many more people— perhaps as many as 15–20% of the population as a whole—have some of the symptoms of dyslexia, including slow or inaccurate reading, poor spelling, poor writing, or mixing up similar words. Not all of these will qualify for special education, but they are likely to struggle with many aspects of academic learning and are likely to benefit from systematic, explicit, instruction in reading, writing, and language. Dyslexia occurs in people of all backgrounds and intellectual levels. People with dyslexia can be very bright. They are often capable or even gifted in areas such as art, computer science, design, drama, electronics, math, mechanics, music, physics, sales, and sports. In addition, dyslexia runs in families; parents with dyslexia are very likely to have children with dyslexia. For some people, their dyslexia is identified early in their lives, but for others, their dyslexia goes unidentified until they get older. |

| AD/HD and dyslexia are distinct conditions that frequently overlap, thereby causing some confusion about the nature of these two conditions. AD/HD is one of the most common developmental problems, affecting 3–5% of the school population. It is characterized by inattention, distractibility, hyperactivity and impulsivity. It is estimated that 30% of those with dyslexia have coexisting AD/HD. Coexisting means the two conditions, AD/HD and dyslexia,can occur together, but they do not cause each other. Dyslexia is a language-based learning disability characterized by difficulties with accurate and fluent word recognition, spelling,and reading decoding. People with dyslexia have problems discriminating sounds within a word or phonemes, a key factor in their reading and spelling difficulties. (See IDA fact sheets [Definition of Dyslexia](https://eida.org/definition-of-dyslexia/) and [Dyslexia Basics](https://eida.org/dyslexia-basics/).) |
